page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.r5.6xlarge is a memory-optimized cloud server built on the x86_64 architecture and managed via the KVM hypervisor. Compute is powered by an Intel Xeon 8163 processor operating at a base frequency of 2.5 GHz. The instance is configured with 24 dedicated virtual CPUs derived from 12 physical cores using two threads per core. Memory capacity is set at 192.0 GB, establishing a 1:8 core-to-memory allocation of 8.0 GB per vCPU. The processor includes 33 MB of L3 cache alongside instruction support for AVX, AVX-512F, AES, and FMA. No dedicated GPUs or local storage devices are included, meaning all persistent storage relies on external network-attached block devices. Network capability provides an 8 Gbps baseline bandwidth without complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark results show balanced multi-threaded performance alongside modest single-threaded throughput. Single-core stress-ng tests place the instance in the lower quartile at 1,108.99, while multi-core stress-ng reaches an average rating of 17,654.0. Single-threaded gzip compression performs in the bottom decile at 18.96 GB/sec, reflecting the lower per-core frequency limits. In contrast, multi-threaded bzip3 decompression scales adequately to 84.54 GB/sec. The PassMark CPU test scores 18,319.89, with extended instruction handling reaching 17,919.11 and database operations registering 6,461.54. Uncached memory bandwidth delivers 97.83 GB/sec for sequential reads and 49.75 GB/sec for writes on 256 MB blocks, supporting 16.79 million Redis SET operations per second.

The qualitative cost-efficiency profile of ecs.r5.6xlarge favors workloads that require dense RAM capacity rather than raw single-core compute performance. Because the instance pairs dedicated multi-core capacity with a high memory ratio, it provides stable resource density for memory-intensive enterprise tasks. Tradeoffs include modest single-thread execution speeds and the absence of attached NVMe storage, requiring architectural reliance on remote volumes for IO-heavy operations. The hardware layout fits production in-memory data grids, Redis and Memcached deployments, distributed caching systems, and medium-scale relational databases.
